directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Victoria is self-fertile and does not require a second variety for pollination, though a pollinator improves yield. The single most widely grown plum in England and one of the best-known European dessert plums in the world, it bears heavy crops of large, oval, red-blushed yellow fruit with juicy, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, and its reliable, self-fertile heavy bearing has made it a standard first-choice plum for a home orchard with room for only one tree. Its very heavy crops often require significant hand thinning of young fruit to prevent limb breakage and to improve the size and quality of the remaining plums. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, thin crowded fruit clusters, and support heavily laden branches in a good fruiting year.

planting.note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; Coe's Golden Drop needs a compatible European plum or gage pollinator and blooms late, helping it dodge some spring frosts.

directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; Coe's Golden Drop needs a compatible European plum or gage pollinator and blooms late, helping it dodge some spring frosts. An English gage-type dessert plum bred in Suffolk in the late eighteenth century, it is celebrated by connoisseurs for exceptionally rich, honeyed, sweet flesh inside a translucent golden-yellow skin often blushed pink in full sun, generally considered one of the finest-flavored dessert plums grown, though the tree is a notoriously shy and unreliable bearer compared to workhorse varieties like Victoria. Its late bloom period helps it escape some late spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering plums, but it still benefits from a warm, sheltered site to ripen its sugars fully and from a compatible pollinator, since it does not reliably self-pollinate. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and be patient with its lighter, less predictable crops in exchange for exceptional dessert flavor.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Czar is self-fertile, reliably productive, and one of the earliest-ripening European plums.

directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Czar is self-fertile, reliably productive, and one of the earliest-ripening European plums. An English culinary plum introduced in the 1870s, it bears heavy, reliable crops of dark purple-black, medium-sized fruit ripening notably earlier in the season than most other European plums, with tart, firm flesh that holds together well for cooking, canning, and jam-making even though it is somewhat less sweet than a fresh-eating dessert plum. Its self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and early ripening have made it a longstanding favorite for a productive, low-maintenance home orchard plum, particularly where an early culinary crop is wanted ahead of the main plum season. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit for better size, since it often sets a very heavy crop.

planting.note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Opal is self-fertile, precocious, and among the earliest dessert plums to ripen.

directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Opal is self-fertile, precocious, and among the earliest dessert plums to ripen. A Swedish-bred dessert plum from a Victoria and Oullins Golden Gage cross, it bears reliably heavy crops of medium, reddish-purple fruit with sweet, juicy, richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening notably early in the plum season, well ahead of Victoria, which makes it a valued choice for extending the home orchard's fresh plum harvest earlier into summer. Its good cold hardiness relative to many English and French plum varieties, combined with reliable self-fertile heavy cropping and precocious young bearing, has made it a popular choice for colder-climate home orchards across northern Europe and the northern United States. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit clusters to improve size in a heavy-cropping year.
